paras: The lynching near Australia Landing, Mississippi, was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a mob of Black men on a plantation in Bolivar County in late March 1888. He had been accused of killing or wounding a popular man during a quarrel at a plantation ball, and friends of the slain man took him and hanged him to a tree on the Mississippi River levee. Memphis reports carried the story to papers in Kentucky and South Carolina, where one account presented it as the work of a 'Band of Black Ku-Klux'.

Australia Landing lay on the river in Bolivar County, and the Memphis Avalanche noted that the area was remote from the telegraph and railroad mail, so its news arrived by the steamer Kate Adams. According to that account, the Black residents of the plantation just south of the landing held a ball about the middle of the week, which ended in a fight among crap shooters.

The reports disagree on what the accused man did. The March 29 Memphis wire said one crap-shooter shot and killed another, while the Avalanche said a shot fired at a winning opponent missed and killed a bystander instantly. A second Memphis dispatch, which placed the events on the Sledge and Mason plantations a few miles below the landing, said instead that the man had cut 'a very popular negro' with a razor over a game.

The Avalanche said the accused was arrested and held in a nearby saloon under a Black officer until he could be taken to the county jail about twenty miles away. The slain man's supporters formed a mob that night but dispersed without acting, then returned the next night, surrounded the saloon, and made the officer give up the prisoner, which he did without resistance. By that account they tied a rope to one of his feet, dragged him across the levee to a tree several hundred yards away, and hanged him by the neck, while the second dispatch said they dragged him by the neck about a hundred yards through a creek and up the levee before hanging him. One version of that dispatch dated the lynching to 'Saturday last', which would be about March 24.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and the victim, the slain man and the officer are not named. The same dispatch also reported a separate killing on those plantations, in which Robert Taylor, a white man, shot and killed a Black man who tried to strike him.

The Maysville Evening Bulletin ran the two-sentence wire on March 29 under the headline 'Negro Murderer Hanged by a Mob', calling the accused 'the murderer'. The second dispatch appeared without comment in the Hopkinsville Semi-weekly South Kentuckian on March 30 and in the Yorkville Enquirer's news column on April 4, where it differed only in calling the game cards rather than craps.

The Manning Times in South Carolina reprinted the Memphis Avalanche's longer account on April 11 under the headline 'Wild Doings in the South. The Bloody Work of a Band of Black Ku-Klux.' That piece described the ball as one of the 'colored fandangoes', called the slain man a 'darky', and depicted the hanging 'amid brutal curses and jeers'. It closed with a partisan point, saying that because both lynchers and victim were Republicans the Northern press would hardly call the hanging a 'Southern outrage', and that the Republicans had lost a voter.

The Avalanche account, which came by steamer from the area and gives the most detail, says the accused killed a bystander by gunfire, the wire says he killed a fellow crap-shooter, and the second dispatch says he cut a man with a razor without stating that the man died. The accounts also differ on the date, with one placing the lynching on a Saturday and the Avalanche placing it on the night after a mid-week ball.

reader.title: Lynching near Australia Landing, Mississippi (1888)
bases: A mob of Black men took a Black man accused of a killing at a plantation ball and hanged him to a tree on the levee (A1, A2, A4).

All reports say the accused man was hanged by a mob or by 'men of his own race' without any legal proceeding, and A4 says the mob took him from an officer holding him for removal to the county jail (A1, A2, A4); the pretext was retribution for the killing or cutting of a popular man (A1, A4).

Three differently worded Memphis reports (the March 29 wire, a second dispatch, and the Memphis Avalanche account) agree that a Black man was hanged by a Black mob on the levee near Australia Landing after violence at a plantation gathering, though they differ on details (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: Memphis wire (March 29)
accounts.gist: At a ball of colored people south of Australia Landing one crap-shooter shot and killed another; friends of the victim secured the killer and hanged him on the levee.

accounts.label: Second Memphis dispatch
accounts.gist: On the Sledge and Mason plantations a man who cut a very popular man with a razor over a game was lynched by men of his own race, dragged by the neck through a creek and up the levee and hanged.

accounts.label: Memphis Avalanche (steamer Kate Adams news)
accounts.gist: A shot fired at a winning crap opponent killed a bystander; the shooter was held in a saloon by a Black officer, and on the second night a mob took him, dragged him by one foot to a tree and hanged him.

framing.detail: Headline 'Negro Murderer Hanged by a Mob' over a two-sentence Memphis wire that calls the accused 'the murderer'.
A brief news paragraph pairing the lynching with a white man's killing of a Black man, without comment.

Headed 'Wild Doings in the South. The Bloody Work of a Band of Black Ku-Klux,' the Avalanche piece uses ridicule ('slain darky', 'colored fandangoes') and turns the lynching into a jab at Republicans and the Northern press.
